theme: Sheba’s revolt; famine; David’s song, the LORD is my rock
readingInstruction: Read 2 Samuel 20:1-22:51. Sheba’s rebellion is put down, and the narrative moves to an appendix that begins with David’s long song of thanksgiving. Notice how the chapters end with praise.
settingTheScene: After David’s return, a worthless man named Sheba leads a revolt of the northern tribes, and Joab murders Amasa and puts it down. Chapters 21 to 24 form an appendix to the book, rather than a chronological narrative, and begin with a famine that David deals with, a list of warriors, and finally the song of chapter 22, which is the same as Psalm 18, which you read earlier.
observation: Sheba says, “We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse” (20:1).
Joab murders Amasa with a sword, and a wise woman of Abel saves her city by persuading the people to throw out Sheba’s head (20:8-22).
A three-year famine comes because of Saul’s bloodguilt against the Gibeonites, and David deals with it (21:1-14).
David’s mighty men kill Philistine giants (21:15-22).
“The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge” (22:2-3).
“He reached down from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters” (22:17).
“This God, his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true” (22:31).
“Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever” (22:51).
interpretation:
The rebellion of Sheba is a short echo of Absalom’s. It shows that the unity of the kingdom is fragile. The cry, “We have no portion in David,” foreshadows the division that will follow Solomon (1 Kings 12:16). Even in David’s restoration, the seeds of the split are visible.

Chapter 21 is hard for modern readers. Saul had violated an ancient oath to the Gibeonites by trying to wipe them out. A famine follows, and David asks God. The solution involves the execution of seven of Saul’s descendants. The chapter shows that sins have long consequences, and that oaths made in God’s name are serious. It also shows David’s care for Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth, whom he spares for the sake of his oath, and his honor for the bones of Saul and Jonathan.

The list of David’s mighty men, and the stories of giants slain, remind us that the kingdom was won by the courage of many. David does not stand alone. He leads a band of faithful warriors. Yet when David grows weary, his men insist that he no longer go out to battle, “lest you quench the lamp of Israel” (21:17). The king’s life is precious because the nation depends on him.

Then comes the song. It is Psalm 18, placed here as a summary of David’s life. The editor of the book wanted readers to look back on everything that had happened and hear David’s own testimony: God rescued me. The song ends with the promise of an everlasting kingdom. The appendix begins with the rock and ends with the offspring of David forever.

The structure is intentional. Between the wars and the failures, the book wants us to see God’s faithfulness. The final word is steadfast love.
connection: Jesus is the “lamp” that does not go out (John 8:12), and the greater king who did not stay home from battle but went to the cross. Paul quotes 2 Samuel 22:50 in Romans 15:9 and applies it to Christ among the Gentiles. The theme of the one who is “rescued out of many waters” finds its fulfillment in the resurrection. Hebrews 11:32-34 recalls David among those who conquered through faith.
application:
Look back over your life and write your own short song of thanks, modeled on 2 Samuel 22.

Ask whether any promise or oath you have made needs to be kept.

Thank God for the people who fight alongside you.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what he has been to you: rock, fortress, deliverer.
Thank him for steadfast love that has not left.
